NEWSPAPERS RECAP

GCSE Media Studies · Component 1 · Section A · The Newspaper Pair

A red-top tabloid recruiting a "Jabs Army" and a broadsheet putting the PM's jogging shorts on page one. Two front pages, two ideologies — learn both inch by inch.

Set text: The Sun — 1 January 2021 Set text: The Guardian — 18 January 2022 Focus: Media Language · Representation · Contexts
01

Tabloids, Broadsheets & Bias

Newspapers come in two main formats — and nearly every ML and representation point flows from which format, and which political allegiance, a paper has.

Tabloid vs Broadsheet — the conventions

Tabloids (e.g. The Sun, Daily Mirror)Broadsheets (e.g. The Guardian, The Times)
"Popular" press · aimed at lower social groupings (C2, D & E)"Quality"/serious press · aimed at higher social groupings (A, B, C1)
Bold layout: big colour on the front page, red mastheads ("red tops"), very bold large typeface, dramatic picturesPlainer layout: little colour, smaller typeface — readers make more effort to read it; subtle, smaller pictures
Shorter articles, more pictures, less in-depth reporting; puns and jokes in headlinesLonger articles, more detail; serious headlines
Human interest stories, celebrity gossip; gimmicks — bingo, free travel, phone-in surveysMore focus on politics and international news
Sensationalist styleRegarded as more serious and less sensationalist
Tabloid: red top, huge headline, celebrity picture
Broadsheet: restrained layout, more text, serious lead

Political bias

UK papers tend to support either right-wing (Conservative) or left-wing (Labour) politics — most visible in reporting of Brexit and elections. A paper's bias affects how events, issues and social groups are represented.

The Sun: right-wing, Conservative-supporting (though it backed Labour in the past — "Boris ticks all the boxes", 2019). The Guardian: left-leaning. The market splits into populars (Sun, Mirror, Star), mid-market (Mail, Express) and quality (Guardian, Times, Telegraph, FT).

Galtung & Ruge — news values (1973)

A set of values acting as gatekeeping: they determine how much prominence a story gets. Think: negativity, unexpectedness, elite persons/nations, personalisation, proximity, continuity, immediacy.

Apply them: the PM lying (elite person + negativity) leads The Guardian; a national vaccine campaign (proximity + positivity + personalisation via celebrities) leads The Sun.

The Sun — industry & audience snapshot

Launched 1964 · News UK (subsidiary of Murdoch's News Corp) · phone-hacking scandal closed the News of the World in 2011, The Sun on Sunday replaced it in 2012 · ~1.3m daily circulation, ~2.2m readership (figures stopped in 2020 — "18 copies a second") · majority male, C2DE, 35–64 · YouGov: ~97% had heard of it… only ~29% liked it

02

The Sun (1 January 2021) — "Join Our Jabs Army"

New Year's Day 2021: Britain is first in the West to license a Covid vaccine, Brexit has just "happened" — and The Sun turns its front page into a recruitment poster.

Spot the detail — the front page up close

Each crop is an exam point. Picture the detail → write the paragraph.

The mastheadRed-top masthead + "The People's Paper" slogan. Beside it, Boris Johnson with a thumbs up: "PM: BRITAIN BREXPECTS" — a pun promising an optimistic Brexit future, and a positive image of the PM that fits The Sun's Conservative support.
The key imageBig Ben's clock face at midnight — New Year, and time ticking. The hands are replaced by a syringe: the vaccine as the nation's fresh start. Iconic British landmark = nationalistic imagery.
The copy"As 2021 dawns, we call on YOU to sign up…" — direct address in capitals, collective pronouns, and an imperative call to action. Informal, urgent, personal.
The headline"JOIN OUR JABS ARMY" — imperative + military metaphor: Covid framed as a war, the enemy to be conquered; "OUR" is protective and unifying. The heart-shaped Union Jack logo stitches patriotism to the campaign.
Opinion leader 1Gary Lineker — Match of the Day presenter, 8.5m followers — "This is a terrific campaign": celebrity endorsement lending credibility (a two-step flow of influence).
Opinion leader 2Kate Garraway — TV presenter whose husband Derek was left seriously ill by Covid — "let's all club together": personal identity appeal; readers know and feel her story.

"Britain Expects" — the intertextual masterstroke

In WW2, Churchill rallied the nation by quoting Admiral Nelson at Trafalgar: "England expects that every man will do his duty." A wartime poster altered it to "Britain expects that you too, this day, will do your duty" — and it has been a tabloid staple ever since.

"BRITAIN BREXPECTS" + the "Jabs Army" recruit-your-country framing deliberately echo this intertextuality: the vaccine campaign becomes a patriotic war effort, and signing up becomes your duty.

The Sun Says column flatters its "fantastic readers" — flattery + "us/we/YOU" throughout positions the audience to share the paper's viewpoint.

Nelson at Trafalgar
The WW2 poster
The Sun Says: "our fantastic readers" — flattery and positioning

Representation & contexts on this page

  • Covid: framed as a war — an enemy to be conquered; the jab as positive, patriotic action (images, language, endorsements all agree). Context: the UK was the first western country to license a vaccine; mass immunisation was essential.
  • Brexit: the off-lead is purely positive — "newfound freedom", "heralded" a "dawn" connoting a great future away from the EU — matching The Sun's right-wing, pro-Leave ideology (2016 referendum: 52/48).
  • Boris Johnson: thumbs up, optimistic — the Conservative PM presented favourably.
  • The readers: represented as an army of willing volunteers — "the People's Paper" mobilising its people.

03

The Guardian (18 January 2022) — "Cummings accuses PM of lying"

Partygate. The broadsheet approach: formal, factual, attributed — and every bit as ideological, just quieter about it.

Spot the detail — the front page up close

The masthead"The Guardian — For 200 years": heritage and trust. "News provider of the year" adds authority. Price: £2.50 (The Sun: 60p) — quality journalism as a paid-for product for an ABC1 audience.
The headline"Cummings accuses PM of lying over No 10 party" — focused and factual, as expected of a quality paper. "Accuses" and "lying" highlight the spat between the PM and his former aide; the accused is the man meant to hold the highest standards. "Party" quietly reinforces the clown image.
The imageThe PM jogging in shorts and a woolly hat — none of the dress codes of a Prime Minister: a representation of lost authority. The caption anchors it: "The prime minister… jogs with his dog, Dilyn" — deadpan, and devastating.
The skylineGiven to the G2 supplement: "What we miss about working in the office" — a lighter alternative to hard news, with intertextuality (The Office) and office-life stereotypes. Note: broadsheets use stereotypes for entertainment features; tabloids use them in lead stories. "We" assumes readers are office workers — post-pandemic WFH culture.
Sub-story 1"UK sending anti-tank weapons to Ukraine" — serious international news, a broadsheet convention. The plain "UK" framing suggests the Guardian (and its readers) support the action.
Sub-story 2"Inquiry launched into Mone over 'VIP lane' deal" — more Conservative dishonesty (a peer not following standards). Story selection does the ideological work.

Representation of politicians — bias without a byline

  • Unlike The Sun (which tells you what it thinks in "The Sun Says"), The Guardian doesn't state an opinion — but the cover is constructed so that every story presents the Conservatives as untrustworthy: lying about parties, VIP-lane deals, standards inquiries.
  • The main image shows a politician with none of the typical costume of a PM — representing a lack of authority and ability.
  • That's the left-leaning ideology at work through selection and construction — a subtler positioning than the tabloid's, and a top-band point when you name it.

Head to Head

The exam loves the contrast. Same country, thirteen months apart — two completely different constructions of Britain.

The two set texts side by side

The Sun (1 Jan 2021)The Guardian (18 Jan 2022)

05 · Comp 1 Sec B

Industry — The Sun & the Newspaper Business

Section B asks stepped questions about The Sun as an industry: who owns it, how it's regulated, and how a 300-year-old form survives the internet.

1964
First published — as a broadsheet with no party allegiance
1969
Bought by Rupert Murdoch — relaunched as a tabloid
1978
UK's biggest-selling paper ever since
2010→
Backing the Conservatives (it has switched sides before — hugely influential at elections)

An industry in decline — and its response

  • Newspapers have existed 300+ years, but sales have fallen hard: competition from online and 24-hour news — free, always updated, personalised, on the phone in your pocket.
  • Warning signs everywhere: The New Day closed nine weeks after launching (2016); The Independent went digital-only.
  • The response: distribute content through websites, social media feeds, apps and downloadable editions — and make money through advertising in print AND online, alongside the cover price.
  • Citizen journalism: the public now collects and reports news (phone footage of storms, attacks) — shifting some control away from big institutions.
The New Day: dead in nine weeks
The Independent: print abandoned

Ownership & control

  • The Sun is owned by News UK, part of the global media conglomerate News Corp — which also owns The Times, The Sunday Times, talkSPORT and Virgin Radio.
  • Concentration of ownership: the three largest publishers own over 70% of UK newspapers — News UK, DMGT (Daily Mail) and Reach plc (the Mirror titles).
  • The Sun and The Times are opposite formats with opposite audiences — same owner. That's the classic exam point about ownership and plurality.
One company: News UK's stable of brands

Gatekeeping — the five sources of news: press releases · news agencies (e.g. Reuters) · global organisations with worldwide branches (BBC, News Corp) · local newspapers · the general public. The editor is the "gatekeeper" who decides what gets in — guided by news values.

Regulation — IPSO

  • Newspapers are regulated by IPSO — the Independent Press Standards Organisation (film = BBFC · games = VSC/PEGI · TV & radio = Ofcom · advertising = ASA).
  • IPSO enforces the Editors' Code of Practice, balancing two things: newspapers' freedom to publish what is in the public interest, and protection of individuals' right to privacy.
  • IPSO was formed after the phone-hacking scandal (and the Leveson Inquiry) — the same scandal that closed the News of the World in 2011, replaced by The Sun on Sunday in 2012.
  • The Sun has fallen foul of IPSO: in 2016 its "Queen backs Brexit" splash was ruled misleading and inaccurate — forcing a front-page correction: "IPSO rules against Sun's Queen headline."
The phone-hacking scandal: the Murdochs face the inquiry that reshaped press regulation

Inside the print edition — the regular features (and why they're there)

  • The masthead — bright, bold, leaning to the right: forward-looking "positivity"; the tagline connotes patriotism.
  • Front page — one main story, puns and hyperbole, large images; a mix of "hard" news (politics) and "soft" (celebrity, human interest).
  • The Sun Says editorial — the paper's official view; celebrity columns; the Bizarre gossip column and TV listings; sports pages at the back, dominated by football.
  • Advertising — well-known high-street brands reflecting the C2DE demographic.
  • Interaction — puzzles, horoscopes, advice columns, readers' letters ("You tell Britain what you think"), Sun Savers offers: readers as participants, not just consumers.

06 · Comp 1 Sec B

Audience — Reaching the SunVerse

The Sun is no longer just a newspaper: it's a print-digital-social brand empire. Audience questions want the numbers, the platforms, and the theory.

The SunVerse — one brand, every platform

Print (The Sun, Sun on Sunday, Fabulous) · Digital (thesun.co.uk, apps, social) · Brand extensions (Sun Bets, Sun Bingo, Dream Team, Sun Savers) — No.1 selling paper (18 a second) · 40M digital reach/month · UK's largest mobile news brand (96% visit by phone) · 16.1M on Facebook & Twitter · 500K a day on Snapchat

Digital convergence — why it matters to The Sun

  • Website, Facebook, Twitter (1.49M followers, updated hourly, separate accounts per section) and a paid app for downloading full editions.
  • Convergence reaches a much wider audience who actively choose how to interact — and the digital audience has a higher income, attracting a more extensive range of advertisers.
  • Share buttons at the bottom of every article turn readers into distributors.
  • UGC — "We pay for your stories!": user-generated content makes readers feel involved and supplies relatable human-interest stories that appeal to people like them.
UGC: readers as reporters
Hourly updates, section-by-section feeds

Why audiences still choose print — and how The Sun appeals

  • Print survives because: the form is familiar; content is organised predictably (news at the front, sport at the back); it needs no internet or device; it fits daily routines (the commute); many prefer paper and in-depth reads.
  • Appealing to the demographic: striking colours, bold headlines, large images, sensational content, less chunky text, puns and wordplay, informal language, offers and freebies.

Uses & Gratifications applied (name a platform in your answer!): Personal identity — human-interest stories readers identify with · Information — news, TV listings · Entertainment/escapism — celebrity gossip, Bizarre · Social interaction — website comments, letters page, sharing stories.

Reception theory: "A Conservative-supporting reader may have a preferred response to The Sun's editorial as it reflects their own ideology" — while a Remain-voting reader may read the same page oppositionally. Audiences are active: they email, comment, join forums, post on social media.

07

Exam-Style Practice

The newspaper ML question follows the familiar pattern — and The Guardian was the text in 2024. Expect: images and/or graphics · layout and design · language/written copy, in [5]/[5]/[5] or [10]/[5] combinations.

Q1 · "Explore how the front page of The Sun uses media language to create meaning: language/written copy [5]"

The imperative headline "JOIN OUR JABS ARMY" commands the reader to act, while the military metaphor frames Covid as an enemy to be defeated — making vaccination a patriotic duty. Collective pronouns ("our", "we") unite paper and reader as one team, and the capitalised direct address "YOU" hands that reader personal responsibility. "Britain BrExpects" adds an intertextual pun on Nelson's "England expects", borrowing wartime connotations of duty, while flattery in The Sun Says ("our fantastic readers") positions the audience to accept the paper's viewpoint.

Q2 · "Explore how the front page of The Guardian uses media language to create meaning: images and/or graphics [10]"

The dominant image shows the Prime Minister jogging in patterned shorts and a woolly hat — none of the dress codes of his office — constructing a representation of lost authority precisely as the headline accuses him of lying. The deadpan caption ("The prime minister… jogs with his dog, Dilyn") anchors the image's meaning: business as usual while the scandal breaks. The restrained, text-heavy layout around it is a broadsheet convention connoting seriousness, while the colourful G2 skyline above uses intertextual images of office life (The Office) to promote lighter content — stereotypes confined to the entertainment feature, not the news. Together, image selection and construction imply the paper's left-leaning view without a single stated opinion.

Q3 (Sec B) · The Industry stepped question

(a) Name who regulates newspapers in the UK [1] · (b) Name two broadsheets [2] · (c) Briefly explain the difference between a tabloid and a broadsheet [4] · (d) Explain how the newspaper industry uses technology to promote its products. Refer to The Sun. [10]

Facing falling print sales, The Sun distributes content across a website (40M monthly reach), social media feeds (16.1M on Facebook and Twitter, hourly updates, section-specific accounts), Snapchat (500K daily) and a paid app for downloading full editions. Digital convergence lets one story be promoted on every platform at once, with share buttons turning readers into distributors and synergy between the paper and website driving audiences both ways. Brand extensions (Sun Bingo, Sun Bets, Dream Team, Sun Savers) monetise the audience beyond news — and the higher-income digital audience attracts a wider range of advertisers.

Q4 (Sec B) · The Audience stepped question

(a) What type of newspaper is The Sun? [1] · (b) Identify one audience for The Sun website [1] · (c) Briefly explain how the content of The Sun website appeals to this audience [4] · (d) Explain why audiences may interpret the same media product in different ways. Refer to The Sun. [12]

Stuart Hall's reception theory: producers encode meaning, but audiences decode it according to their own experiences and beliefs. A Conservative-supporting, working-class reader may take the preferred reading of The Sun's Jabs Army front page — a patriotic, unifying campaign. A reader who distrusts the paper's politics may negotiate: supporting vaccination while rejecting the jingoistic framing. An oppositional reader — perhaps someone alienated by the paper's history or its Brexit stance — may see manipulation and propaganda. Factors shaping these readings include politics, age, class, and personal experience of the pandemic (e.g. readers who identified with Kate Garraway's story). Audiences are also active — commenting, sharing and even contributing stories — so meaning is never simply received.

The 25-marker (Sec A) · compare representation with an unseen front page

Same method as every form: ~10 minutes annotating the unseen text first · Intro → rep in the set text → rep in the unseen → similarities → differences → conclusion · use the terminology (masthead, skyline, splash, anchorage, positioning, gatekeeping, news values) and name the ideology.
